title: Ring-oscillator PUF (pairwise oscillator-frequency-comparison identity primitive)
topology: A bank of nominally identical ring oscillators laid out identically across the die; a challenge selects a pair of oscillators, their frequencies are counted over a fixed interval, and a comparator emits one response bit from the sign of the frequency difference. Because each ring's frequency is set by its own manufacturing mismatch, which of a pair is faster is device-unique, repeatable, and unclonable — a Physical Unclonable Function response usable for authentication and, with a fuzzy extractor, key generation. Comparing pairs (rather than reading absolute frequency) cancels shared temperature/voltage/aging drift to first order, making the response far more stable than an absolute-frequency measurement. This is the oscillator-frequency-comparison counterpart to the SRAM power-up PUF and reuses the same ring-oscillator building block as the jitter TRNGs, but here the deterministic mismatch (not the jitter) is the signal.
spec_class: hardware security primitive — Physical Unclonable Function for device authentication and secret-key generation, where a device-unique, drift-tolerant unclonable identity is derived from ring-oscillator frequency mismatch rather than stored in nonvolatile memory; the design must supply a stable, reproducible response plus error-correction handling, not any analog-precision or phase-noise spec

pdk_portability.notes: Fully digital-standard-cell portable: the primitive needs only inverter/NAND ring oscillators, counters, and a comparator, all in sky130's standard-cell library (sky130_fd_sc_hd) and every digital CMOS PDK. What is PDK-specific is the frequency-mismatch distribution between nominally identical rings (set by the node's device-mismatch statistics), which determines how reliably a pair's ordering can be resolved and thus the response bit-error-rate; this must be characterized on sky130 silicon across temperature/voltage/aging. Response stability and the fraction of usable (well-separated) oscillator pairs must be measured on the target PDK to size error correction; do not port a BER or entropy figure from another node or from an FPGA implementation, and note that FPGA RO-PUFs need placement constraints that are moot in a full-custom/standard-cell ASIC flow.

sizing_approach: Because the PUF exploits intrinsic mismatch, the rings are deliberately built from identical instances rather than custom-sized; the design work is at the system level. Size the number of oscillators (and hence the number of comparable pairs / challenge-response space) large enough to yield the required number of stable response bits after discarding close-frequency (unreliable) pairs and applying error correction. Set the frequency-count interval long enough that the counter resolution reliably distinguishes a matched pair's small frequency difference above measurement noise, trading response time against reliability. Size the fuzzy-extractor / error-correcting code to the worst-case measured intra-device BER (over temperature, voltage, aging) so the reconstructed key is reliable while helper data leaks acceptably little entropy; a common robustness technique selects, per device at enrollment, only pairs whose frequency separation exceeds a guard band. Provision spare oscillators for enrollment discards and aging margin.
layout_idioms: lay out all ring oscillators identically (same cells, orientation, routing, and local environment) so their nominal frequencies match and the response comes from random device mismatch rather than systematic layout differences
compare oscillators in pairs so shared temperature/voltage/aging drift is common-mode-cancelled to first order, which is the key to a stable, reproducible response
prefer comparing physically adjacent oscillators (or select pairs at enrollment) so correlated systematic gradients cancel and only random mismatch — the unclonable part — remains as signal
keep enrollment/reconstruction, helper-data, and the derived key on an access-controlled path separate from scan/debug, and provide a raw frequency-count read path for characterization only

source.citation: G. E. Suh and S. Devadas, "Physical Unclonable Functions for Device Authentication and Secret Key Generation," Proceedings of the 44th Design Automation Conference (DAC), pp. 9-14, 2007 (author-hosted preprint publicly available). Error-correction/fuzzy-extractor context: J. Guajardo, S. S. Kumar, G.-J. Schrijen, and P. Tuyls, "FPGA Intrinsic PUFs and Their Use for IP Protection," CHES 2007.
source.license_or_openness: Suh-Devadas is cited for its ring-oscillator PUF (pairwise frequency-comparison) topology and methodology only (no figures or text reproduced); an author-hosted (MIT CSAIL) preprint is publicly available (case 1 open-access), with the ACM/IEEE DAC proceedings version behind a subscription (case 2). Guajardo et al. is cited (case 2) for the fuzzy-extractor methodology. No proprietary or NDA'd data is recorded.

notes: The RO-PUF's stability advantage comes entirely from the pairwise, difference-based readout — comparing two on-die oscillators cancels the environmental drift that would wreck an absolute-frequency measurement. As with the SRAM PUF, a fuzzy extractor / error-correcting code is required to turn the noisy response into a reproducible key, and helper data must be designed to leak little entropy; response drift over temperature, voltage, and aging sets the error-correction budget and must be measured on silicon. This entry shares the ring-oscillator building block with ring-oscillator-jitter-trng and multi-ro-xor-entropy-source, but there the exploited signal is stochastic jitter, whereas here it is the deterministic per-ring frequency mismatch; see sram-power-up-puf for the memory-based unclonable-identity alternative.

artifacts.notes: From-scratch netlist (real sky130_fd_pr__nfet_01v8/pfet_01v8 devices, not behavioral), two free-running 5-stage ring oscillators built per this entry's own topology text. Because a single deterministic SPICE run has no per-instance random mismatch, ring B's five stages are all drawn a deterministic 5% wider (both NMOS and PMOS) than ring A's as a stand-in for the random manufacturing mismatch a real RO-PUF exploits -- exactly the same simplification sram-power-up-puf/sram_cell_powerup.spice uses for its own bistable-resolution mismatch. The measured sign of the frequency difference (ring B faster) is a property of this injected asymmetry's sign, not a prediction of any real device pair's response; mirroring the asymmetry onto ring A instead flips the sign. This testbench also measures each ring's period directly via SPICE .meas TRIG/TARG timing rather than building the entry's own counter+comparator digital back-end, which would add digital complexity without changing what is being verified here (that a small drawn-width mismatch resolves to a measurable, repeatable frequency ordering). A real bit-error-rate/response-stability distribution needs Monte Carlo over sky130's mismatch models across temperature/voltage/aging, which this single deterministic corner does not do.

measured.notes: Real sky130A device models (volare-fetched, open_pdks), not behavioral elements. Reproduce with `klt sim examples/kb/ro-puf/request.json`. freq_a_hz/freq_b_hz are each ring's own frequency, counted over 8 oscillation periods starting 5ns after the transient begins (letting both rings settle out of their seeded startup transient). freq_diff_hz and freq_diff_pct are ring B minus ring A: positive, as expected, since ring B's devices are drawn 5% wider (more drive current, shorter per-stage delay) -- this is the deterministic mismatch stand-in described in artifacts.notes, not a measured statistic over a random device population. NO bit-error-rate, min-entropy, or response-stability claim is made -- see artifacts.notes for what a real characterization would require (Monte Carlo over sky130's mismatch models across temperature/voltage/aging).
